props.title: It's Alive

sections.content: Larry Cohen's It's Alive revolutionized killer baby movies by injecting social commentary into B-movie horror. The film follows the Davies family whose newborn mutant child goes on a murderous rampage, reflecting 1970s anxieties about birth defects from environmental pollution and pharmaceuticals. Cohen's brilliant stroke was treating the material seriously - Frank Davis (John Ryan) evolves from wanting to destroy his monstrous offspring to protecting it, making this as much about parental love as horror. Bernard Herrmann's haunting score (one of his last) elevates the film above typical creature features.

sections.content: The success of It's Alive spawned two sequels - It Lives Again (1978) and It's Alive III: Island of the Alive (1987), both directed by Cohen. While neither matched the original's impact, they expanded the mythology by showing more mutant babies and exploring government conspiracy angles. The film's influence can be seen in later evil child movies like Grace (2009) and Antibirth (2016), though few match Cohen's ability to blend social commentary with exploitation thrills.

Beyond just killer baby films, It's Alive fits into the broader 1970s eco-horror movement alongside films like Prophecy (1979) and Food of the Gods (1976). These movies channeled growing environmental concerns into monster movies, using mutated creatures as metaphors for humanity's tampering with nature. Cohen's film stands out for focusing on the personal trauma rather than just the carnage. SUBHEAD: The Legacy of It's Alive

sections.content: While modern audiences might find the practical effects dated, It's Alive's themes of parental anxiety and medical distrust remain relevant. The film's DNA can be found in body horror classics like The Fly (1986) and modern parenthood nightmares like The Babadook (2014). Rick Baker's innovative creature design for the murderous infant influenced decades of movie monsters, proving you don't need a huge budget for effective practical effects.
